CANADA COUNCIL CULTURAL GRANTS
speechtext: What grants, expenditures or contributions have been made by the Canada Council for bursaries, scholarships, fellowships and for encouragement of the arts and other cultural activities for 1962, 1963, 1964 and 1965 in each province of Canada and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of Stale):
subtopic: CANADA COUNCIL CULTURAL GRANTS
speechtext:
The Canada Council has provided the following answer: As these statistics had not been developed in the past, the council had a special review made of its existing records and files. The survey has established that the various expenditures of the council cannot be summarized in the form requested, for the following main reasons:
(1)	Although the exact fraction cannot be determined, as much as one third of the council's grants to organizations (such as for interprovincial touring, national conferences, projects or services, etc.) cannot be said to have been spent in any one province in particular;
(2)	In the case of some two thirds of the awards made to individuals, the province of application and award (not to speak of the province of domicile) differs from the place where the applicant wishes to spend the award;
(3)	While records have been kept of all awards made, it is not possible to retrace all the requests which have been made and have determined the council's response, so that essential information on the ratio of approvals to applications is not available.
Following the survey just completed, the council is taking steps to develop various forms of statistical information and analysis which would provide meaningful additions to future annual reports.

subtopic: NATIONAL CLEAN-UP CAMPAIGN
NATIONAL CLEAN-UP CAMPAIGN
speechtext: Has the government received representations regarding a campaign of beautification and clean-up across Canada on the occasion of Expo '67, and especially regarding the elimination of slums along railway lines, the elimination of heaps of refuse, and the encouragement of repair and painting of railway stations and beautification of their approaches?

subtopic: NATIONAL CLEAN-UP CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Yes. The centennial commission has had inquiries from the provinces, from municipalities and from professional and service organizations about a nationally supported program for community improvement and beautification. The inquiries have shown widespread concern for community improvement together with requests for guidance and assistance in the implementation of community improvement projects.
The centennial commission is developing a national community improvement program which represents the call to action for Canadians to improve the appearance of their
Questions
urban and rural environment. This program was actively initiated by the centennial commission in mid-1965 with the first national seminar ever held in Canada on the subject of community improvement and beautification, when guide lines were established for the community improvement program. The second seminar held in Ottawa on April 22, 1966 had as its theme the "Call to Action" for Canadians to embark on a campaign of clean up, paint up, landscaping, beautification and over-all improvement of our surroundings.
The role of the centennial commission is to co-ordinate and direct a community improvement program through the provinces to every municipality or rural area in Canada. The centennial commission is preparing information and guidance material on community improvement for widespread distribution and will give professional assistance wherever possible as a means toward encouraging the implementation of local projects for 1967 and beyond.
This national program has been initiated by the centennial commission on the occasion of the centennial of the confederation and not specially on the occasion of Expo '67.

subtopic: DIRECT SHIPMENTS UNDER CANADA-WEST INDIES AGREEMENT
DIRECT SHIPMENTS UNDER CANADA-WEST INDIES AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Were any exemptions from article VII of the Canada-West Indies agreement of 1925 with regard
[Miss LaMarsh.l
to direct shipments, requested within the last 10 years and, if so, by whom and with what result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DIRECT SHIPMENTS UNDER CANADA-WEST INDIES AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Article VII of the agreement provided for a direct shipment requirement for West Indian goods coming to Canada and permitted the West Indies to impose a similar requirement on Canadian goods going to the West Indies. None of the West Indian authorities have imposed this requirement on Canadian goods during the last 10 years.
The following exceptions have been made by Canada to the direct shipment requirement imposed under article VII of the Canada-West Indies trade agreement in the last 10 years:
(a)	Order in council P.C. 1960-1044, July 30, 1960, permitted the transshipment at Cristobal in the Panama Canal zone of coffee, pimento, ground and unground ginger, lime juice, rum and tia maria, produced in Jamaica, without being subject to the higher most favoured nation rates of customs duty, provided such goods were shipped on a through bill of lading from Jamaica to a port in British Columbia and entered British Columbia by sea. (Requested by Jamaica).
(b)	Order in council P.C. 1961-1675 of November 23, 1961, permitted transshipment of the goods listed in P.C. 1960-1044 at Cristobal or Curacao in the Dutch West Indies. (Requested by Jamaica).
(c)	Order in council P.C. 1964-1759 of November 13, 1964, extended the privilege of transshipment at Cristobal or Curacao to all Jamaican goods. As provided for in the earlier orders, these goods had to be shipped on a through bill of lading from Jamaica to a port in British Columbia and enter British Columbia by sea. (Requested by Jamaica).
(d)	Order in council P.C. 1963-62 of January 10, 1963, permitted the transshipment at Cristobal or Curacao of rum produced in British Guiana if this product was shipped on a through bill of lading from British Guiana to a port in British Columbia and entered British Columbia by sea. (Requested by British Guiana).
(e)	The protocol to the 1925 trade agreement signed at the Commonwealth Caribbean-Canada conference in July 1966 provided for the waiving of the direct shipment requirements of article VII. This undertaking was implemented by Canada under order in council P.C. 1966-1419 of July 27, 1966, which permits goods grown, produced or manufactured in Antigua, the Bahamas, Barbados, Bermuda, British Honduras, Dominica, Gre-

nada, Guyana, Jamaica, Montserrat, St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Trinidad and Tobago, Turks and Caicos Islands and Virgin islands, which are shipped on a through bill of lading to a consignee in a specified port in Canada to be transshipped without becoming subject to the higher most favoured nation rates of customs duty. (Requested by the Commonwealth Caribbean countries as a group).

subtopic: STRATEGIC MATERIALS SUPPLIED FOR U.S. USE IN VIET NAM
speechtext:

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to move, seconded by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North, the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely the action of the Canadian automobile companies in violating both the spirit and the terms of the Can-ada-U.S. automobile trade agreement, and their action in failing to honour solemn commitments made to parliament on their behalf, resulting in lay-offs and dislocation affecting employees, and excessive car prices to the consumer public.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the hon. member kindly address the Chair and the house on the question of urgency of debate?

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that the general question of urgency here cannot be denied in any way. Our latest information indicates that over 5,000 Canadians have been laid off as a result of the dislocations taking place under this pact.
Further with regard to the urgency of debate I would point out that this is the first opportunity that anyone has had to raise this important matter before Your Honour. With respect to further debate upon it, we are told we are now going into debate on the Bank Act and medicare, which debates will be prolonged and will not provide an opportunity for important matters such as this to be raised.
The real urgency of debate lies in what appears to me to be a complete flouting by the Canadian automobile companies of the expressed wishes of this parliament. All of us who followed the debate on the automobile pact legislation recall the solemn assurances made by various ministers to the members of the house that very substantial steps would be taken and machinery would be set up to take care of the dislocations and hardships which we all knew were going to come about as a result of the legislation. In actual fact this has not been done. The motor companies have never participated in the particular form of adjustment assistance outlined. In short they have declined to do so and have thumbed their noses at parliament.
October 5, 1966
The urgency further lies in the fact that if outside individuals and companies are going to go their own way, are going to flout their undertakings to parliament, and are going to disregard the expressed wishes of parliament asserted in legislation, then it is important that we discuss important matters of this kind. I further suggest that the failure of the government to make changes mandatory has permitted the motor companies to thumb their noses at us and has caused resultant great hardship to people in the industry. I know there is the other consideration of differences in price as between the United States and Canada. Your Honour may say that matter will be investigated by a particular committee, and I hope the members of that committee will call representatives of the motor companies before them to justify their actions, but in the light of all these circumstances I submit there is urgency of debate on the matter I have raised.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly in regard to the urgency of debate. Debate should be allowed in order that certain facts may be brought before the people of this country. I would point out that some manufacturers of automobiles under this new agreement are now manufacturing models in the United States which heretofore were built in Canada, and these models are being brought into this country and sold at Canadian prices even though in the United States they are sold at American prices. This, coupled with the fact that the dislocation in the industry is causing a tremendous number of layoffs in the Canadian labour force, merits consideration of the matter by the house.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer some suggestions for your consideration when you are deciding whether or not there is urgency of debate respecting the matter raised by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott).
First of all, Mr. Speaker, citation 100 in Beauchesne's fourth edition states that adjournment of the house under standing order 26 "must involve the administrative responsibility of the government." I do not suppose it could be argued that a change in the price to purchasers of automobiles, whether it be this year or any other year, directly involves the administrative responsibility of the government, except for the fact that during the past 12 months, and even prior to that the government, or I should say parliament, has allowed
Motion for Adjournment something like $50 million per year to be retained in the hands of the automobile manufacturers by relieving them of some import duty, on the firm understanding that there was to be a closing of the gap between the prices of automobiles in Canada and prices in the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the press reports we have had recently are correct regarding the price changes in the United States and the price changes in Canada, there appears to be only a very small amount, something like $17 to $20, in closing the gap between the price in the United States and the price in Canada for a comparable automobile. In line with what has been advanced to the members of this house so far as the agreement is concerned, to the effect that these price differentials would be brought into line by the end of 1968, and the fact that these are the prices for the 1967 models, it seems to me that what the automobile manufacturers are doing in Canada is not in keeping with the spirit and the intent of what was presented to this house. To that extent, Mr. Speaker, in my view it seems that this does involve the administrative responsibility of the government, because we were told this price differential would be eliminated and in exchange $50 million was granted to the automobile manufacturers.
In so far as paragraph 2 of citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition is concerned, it says that a matter must be so pressing that the public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention. Well, Mr. Speaker, the increases in price which have been announced may not be a severe hardship when they amount to somewhere between $40 and $55, but the fact is that the public immediately will begin to pay this amount. Therefore it seems to me it is going to affect the public immediately, whether or not it can be said that the public will suffer. Certainly, however, we have the right to expect an explanation and, as the hon. member for Danforth said, this is the first opportunity we have had to discuss it.
In respect of paragraph 3 of citation 100 dealing with the matter of urgency, where it says there must be urgency of debate, so far as I can see there is no way of bringing parliament's opinion to the attention of the automobile manufacturers in Canada other than through some government sponsored amendment or through a debate in this house. To date we have not had any indication that the government intends to take any action to give effect to what we thought was the intent

8342	COMMONS
Motion for Adjournment and the end result of the agreement that was entered into.
So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer these suggestions for your consideration respecting this whole matter. In summary, it seems to me there has not been the kind of action taken that was promised to close the differential between prices here and in the United States. It seems to me the increase in prices in the model year 1967 is in complete contradiction to what the Minister of Industry said some time ago when explaining certain parts of the agreement. He said that while he could not guarantee there would be an immediate reduction in the prices of Canadian automobiles, it would keep the prices from going up between now and 1968, and that by 1968 the cars in both countries would be at the same price. Now, Mr. Speaker, we have a positive indication that the manufacturers have in fact increased the prices between the time of the agreement and 1968, and therefore there does seem to be a justification for some debate on the matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
As I appreciate the situation, Mr. Speaker, there cannot be any denial of the fact that there is an urgency to discuss this matter. It seems that in view of the agenda announced by the government there will be no discussion of this agreement which was entered into, but it is of interest to note that its results are exactly those predicted by this party before the agreement took effect.
As a result of this agreement between the two countries the Canadian consumers will have to bear an expense of $50 million without receiving any advantage. The Canadian consumer will have to pay more for his car this year than he paid last year, and the only explanation given is that certain safety features will be standard equipment on this year's cars. Surely this additional cost cannot be justified in those terms. This government, by entering into this agreement, has sold out the rights of Canadians.
As a result of this agreement, cars manufactured in Canada are selling in the United States, in competition with cars manufactured there, at lower prices than Canadian consumers are paying. The first commitment which was made was that as a result of this agreement, which gives to the automobile companies some $50 million a year in tax relief, the employees in the automotive manufacturing industry would not suffer and there would be transitional assistance benefits payable to any of those who were thrown out of work. One of the automobile companies, General Motors, has taken the position that it is not required to pay the transitional assistance benefits unless the worker can show that the lay-off is attributable to the Canada-United States auto agreement. Consequently these men are being denied something which was promised them in this house.
I submit that the matter is pressing and ought to be settled now. Many of these men have been laid off and others have been notified that they will be laid off. Unless this parliament acts, and acts promptly, these men will not have any recourse to the assistance which we were told in this house by the government spokesman they would be entitled to receive.
The other commitment which was made by the government on behalf of the automobile companies was that the spread between the prices of cars to the consumers in the United States and Canada would be progressively reduced. The prices were not reduced for the
1966	cars, and the figures announced for the
1967	cars show that prices will be increased and not decreased.
The minister argues that there is a committee of the house looking into the matter of automobile prices. First of all, Mr. Speaker, the committee has not yet agreed to look into the price of cars in Canada; and second, the Canada-United States agreement is not before that committee. It is this house which must deal with the problem. It was this house which passed a resolution authorizing the government to proceed with an agreement which they had entered into some 15 months previously, and it is this house which must accept the responsibility of bringing the government to account if the commitments made under that agreement are not being lived up to by the companies concerned.
October 5, 1966
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that if the 1967 cars go on the market at the prices which have been announced, it will be too late six months from now for the government to take some action with respect to the prices of cars. I therefore claim that this is a matter of urgency which must be dealt with now. If it is not dealt with immediately, certainly both the workers concerned and the consumers of cars will be ill treated and will suffer loss as a result of the failure of this parliament to deal with the present situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-222, respecting Banks and Banking.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preceding this bill was introduced in July, the proposed changes as compared with the present Bank Act were, in my opinion, of such importance that I gave a somewhat fuller and more detailed explanation of the major features than is usually given at the resolution stage. Because of this I do not propose to speak at great length on this bill at the present time. I will of course be pleased to offer any further explanations hon. members may ask for.
As I mentioned in my speech to the house in July, the main proposals contained in this bill to revise the Bank Act are intended to increase the degree of competition and flexibility in our banking system so that it will best serve the changing requirements of the Canadian economy and the interests of all Canadians. This objective was the central theme of the report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, and I believe that the present bill is a very substantial step along the general lines of that commission's recommendations.
These main proposals can be briefly summarized as follows:
(1)	A new formula, effective January 1, 1967, to fix the maximum rate of interest that banks may charge on loans in Canada and eventually to remove the ceiling altogether. The maximum rate for each six months period beginning January 1 and July 1 would be 1J per cent plus the average yield on short term government bonds (i.e. those maturing within three years) during the three months

October 5. 1966
Bank Act
period ending one month before the effective dates. When the average yield on these bonds for any three month period after January 1, 1967, falls below 4J per cent there will no longer be any statutory maximum rate of interest on bank loans in Canada.
(2)	Agreements between banks on interest rates both on loans and deposits will be prohibited.
(3)	Each bank will be required to disclose in its financial statements, details of revenues and expenses and the amount of its so-called inner reserves.
(4)	The present cash reserve requirement of 8 per cent of total Canadian deposits will be gradually replaced by a cash requirement of 12 per cent against demand deposits and 4 per cent against term and notice deposits (including personal savings deposits). On present figures this formula would result in an over-all cash requirement of 6.6 per cent. The Bank of Canada will have stand-by power to impose a secondary reserve, initially of not more than 6 per cent, which may be increased monthly in steps to a maximum of 12 per cent and which the bank may reduce or remove at any time.
(5)	Banks will be permitted to make mortgage loans (N.H.A. and conventional), and the maximum rate of interest provisions will not apply to such loans.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The amount of a conventional mortgage loan will be limited to 75 per cent of the value of the property. The total amount of conventional mortgage loans on residential property that a bank may have will be limited to 3 per cent of its deposit liabilities and debentures in the first year, and 1 additional per cent per annum thereafter, with a maximum of 10 per cent in total.
(6)	The banks are to be given authority to issue debentures ranking in priority after their deposit liabilities. The amount of debentures that a bank may have outstanding will be limited by restricting the increase per annum to 10 per cent of paid-up capital and rest fund, and by an upper limit of one half of a bank's paid-up capital and rest fund.
(7)	The shareholding that a bank may have in any other Canadian corporation is limited to 10 per cent of the voting shares of the other corporation, and no more than one fifth of the directors of any company may become directors of a bank.
(8)	Two years after the statutory interest rate ceiling on bank loans has been removed,
[Mr. Sharp.!
a director of a trust or loan company that accepts deposits from the public may not be appointed or elected a director of a bank.
(9)	Except for any existing situations, and in the case of resident shareholders of a new bank if the government gives specific approval, ownership by any one shareholder and associates will be limited to 10 per cent of a bank's shares, and total ownership by non-residents will be limited to 25 per cent. Pension and similar funds of a province will be permitted to own up to 10 per cent of a bank's shares for all such funds of any province, on a non-voting basis. The size of a bank in which one shareholder has more than a 25 per cent interest will be limited by reference to the amount of its authorized capital and this, as the house knows, applies to the Mercantile Bank, and to another bank which I shall mention shortly.
In that connection I should mention that the special act of parliament incorporating the Bank of Western Canada included limitations similar to those proposed in the bill to revise the Bank Act. The Bank of Western Canada has asked the government for permission to have a group of associated Canadian shareholders hold more than 10 per cent of the bank's initial capital, and that permission has been given by the government. This action, of course, was provided for in the bank's act of incorporation. So long as one shareholder has more than a 25 per cent interest, the Bank of Western Canada will of course be limited as to the size of its operations by reference to the amount of its authorized capital, just as the Mercantile Bank is today.
As I announced in July, legislation to establish a system of deposit insurance for banks, and federally incorporated trust and loan companies, which would be made available to provincially incorporated institutions which accept deposits from the public and carry on business within the meaning of the Trust Companies Act or the Loan Companies Act, is being prepared.
The government will discuss the position of provincially incorporated institutions in relation to deposit insurance with the provincial governments. The intention of the government is to introduce this legislation into parliament as soon as possible in the present session. It would be premature to forecast details at this stage, but I can say that it is the intention that the government will provide the initial capital resources of the insurance corporation, with further resources to be
October 5, 1966

provided by premiums payable by the member institutions. It is the intention to keep these premiums as low as is consistent with establishing an adequate reserve fund against possible losses.
When the resolution for the bill to revise the Bank Act was introduced in July there were some who expressed the view that the government should have defined the business of banking and forced so-called "near banks" either to accept such federal control or give up their banking activities.
My predecessor, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), made clear last year that the determination of what constituted the field of banking within our jurisdiction was a matter for the courts, and it did not appear that the royal commission proposal for treating all institutions accepting deposits payable within a hundred days as banks fitted into the pattern of judicial decisions in this field. We do not think it necessary or desirable at this time to endeavour to force provincial institutions under this somewhat doubtful boundary of our jurisdiction. We think it more sensible to make it possible for the deposit institutions under federal law to be competitive and flexible in meeting the banking requirements of the Canadian people. We believe this will bring about a situation where those who wish to engage in the business of banking will find it to their advantage to come under federal legislation.
I make these comments because this point was urged quite strongly, particularly by members of the official opposition, and I have no doubt urged in good faith, and I am giving the reply in as precise terms as I can as to why we did not at this time proceed to follow the recommendation of the royal commission in this respect. But I would add one word-

speechtext: May I ask a question at this point? Could the minister give us an idea of the extent of the consideration given to the question of a definition of banking that would be acceptable in accordance with the B.N.A. Act? I know it is a difficult problem, but was it considered and rejected as being impractical, or what considerations were involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Advice was sought from the government advisers, from the Department of Justice, and there was a good deal of doubt expressed as to what was or would be an acceptable definition of banking. I believe that it would be desirable, if possible, to establish more clearly the jurisdiction of parliament in this field. On the other hand I
Bank Act
share with my predecessor in office the conviction that it would be rather imprudent on the part of the government to rest its legislation, namely this Bank Act, upon a definition that had to be tested in the courts.
We therefore felt it would make for greater progress in improving the rules for banking business generally, whether one includes the charter banks or "near banks," by establishing a deposit insurance institution.
Until the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) interrupted me I was going to go on to make one other point that was made by the royal commission, because I examined its report after listening to my hon. friends' comments when the resolution stage was under consideration. The royal commission said that there was no particular relationship between removing the interest rate, which they advocated, and the extension of the jurisdiction of parliament over the "near banks." Indeed, as I recall the words of the royal commission, they were to the effect that whatever else is done the interest rate ceiling should be removed.
There has been some criticism made to me by Canadians of the omission from the bill of any provision to permit the establishment of agencies in Canada for foreign banks, as recommended by the royal commission. We have omitted it on the ground that it would weaken in some degree the control exercised over credit conditions in Canada by the monetary authorities. Canada already has a very free and open capital and money market, and Canadians are quite prepared to conduct a large part of their business in other currencies.
On the other hand it has been represented to me that by permitting agencies we would be furthering still more our objective of more competition in lending in Canada, while it would not be necessary to permit the agencies to accept deposits from Canadians, just as the agencies of Canadian banks in, for example, New York, are not permitted to accept deposits from residents of that state. I hope that the committee will go into this subject thoroughly, and I can assure the house that the government will give most serious consideration to its recommendations.
In the weeks since this bill to revise the Bank Act was made public there has been an opportunity for comment and technical criticism, and for consultation, as a result there will be a number of technical points on which the government will propose amendments in committee. When the bill receives second

Mr. Speaker, I did not participate in the debate on resolution stage, because of the time element. The time element is now very critical since the bill must receive consideration by the house on second reading and then must go to a committee where representations will be heard, and time must be allowed to various witnesses, who undoubtedly will wish to appear, to prepare and file their briefs. Then, after consideration by the committee, the bill must come back into this house for clause by clause study in committee of the whole. It must then go to the other place for equal consideration. There is a deadline of November 30 for proclamation. Unless the government brings in a further bill extending the life not. only of the Bank Act but also of the Quebec Savings Bank Act, then our banking operations in this country will cease. I am not very sanguine about any rapid progress. Therefore, I should like to see this bill go through the committee as soon as possible. This is the wish of the official opposition. We made our points at the time of the resolution and, after having seen the bill, I can assure the minister and the government that the views of the opposition have not changed one iota in respect of this bill.
This bill is probably one of the most momentous we have had to study. In so far as Canada and its economic life is concerned, it is even more important than any of the wide ranging proposals for social welfare that the government has considered in the past. It is much more important, in my mind, than the very complex and very important transportation legislation which is before this house at the present time. This bill, and the banking system which must follow upon the implementation of the bill, if passed by parliament, will affect the whole lifeblood of our country. It goes to the absolute root of our economic strength and one can cry or proclaim from the rooftops, or boast about our welfare measures and all sorts of legislation which we may have on our books, but if we have sapped the economic strength of our country, those social welfare measures of our country are not worth the paper they are written on. Therefore, of primary importance to this country is a strong effective banking system, and this is what we must aim for-a strong and effective banking system that not
(Mr. Sharp.]
only sees to the protection of the depositors and the creditors of the banks, but which also is very flexible.
Some may say there is a paradox, there is a conflict of interest at some point; but surely as a result of the studies by the Porter royal commission and the experience of the banking system as a whole, we know at about what point we can reconcile the degrees of flexibility with the appropriate safeguards for the depositors and creditors of our banking institutions. The minister has repeated at the resolution stage, and my colleagues in July indicated a general agreement, that the central theme of the Porter commission report is to allow our financial institutions, especially the chartered banks, to have much broader investment powers and opportunities, coupled with correspondingly broader borrowing powers than existed in 1964. In a nutshell, Canada's banking system must be made more flexible, albeit at the same time maintaining the sound characteristics which have been the hallmark of Canadian banking in the past.
At the resolution stage the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) as well as my colleagues from Perth (Mr. Monteith), Northumberland (Mr. Hees), and Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) emphasized that the recommendations of the Porter commission dealing with this theme were not divisible; they were part of a package which was meant to be all-embracing to cover the bank and "near banks". It is a very poor thing to tinker with the status and powers of banks and leave untended, uncontrolled or unsupervised the activities of the "near banks" which have introduced, if I may use the term, many loose ends in the banking and monetary system of Canada today.
It is singular that we have not heard from the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), who was the godfather and sponsor of the government bill last year, to see what his views would be in respect of the Bank Act, in the light of the debacle of the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation and those companies which went down with it. At that time he held certain airy views, and I thought they were rather casual, with regard to some of the responsibilities under our banking system.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) uses the words "the events of the past year have caused us to revise our thinking". I should hope so; but unfortunately he has gone but an inch when he should have gone a mile. I and my colleagues have stated that we think this is a poor job of tinkering, because
October 5, 1966

the "near banks" who have taken such a large share in the monetary operations in this country are frankly under little or no supervision. I had the opportunity recently to discuss this with a number of the supervisory officers of provincial authorities. Frankly, outside of filing annual returns of a very nominal nature and outside of certain superintendents of insurance adopting an absolute and firm attitude of no expansion into other provinces by provincially incorporated trust companies, there is no control.
It is my thought that there should have been some very positive effort. The deposit insurance scheme advanced by the minister under this act is a form of negative action. I do not see how it will achieve the result we want, which is the protection of the depositors and creditors of these trust companies. Those are the people who have to be protected. Any well-operated trust company would have nothing to fear in operating under the umbrella of the Bank Act. As a matter of fact the officers of a number of these companies have told me they would welcome such control, because it would establish their companies as being well operated and sound companies. I think the banks themselves would not object to it; they would all be on the same footing. I would think that the officers of any chartered bank would tell you they are prepared to compete with anybody, on equal terms.
This is what we must have, but we do not get it in this Bank Act. We know there are some operations which would have difficulty standing up to the light of day. In the last week I have seen in the windows of a trust company a new advertisement announcing 1i per cent deposit certificates.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
There is an interest spread between 7J per cent and 6J per cent, because the standard interest rate on this type of investment on the part of provincial and trust companies is about 61 per cent or 6J per cent, although some limit the rate to 6} per cent. I should like the Minister of Finance to tell this house what he thinks the rate on the return of investment in these trust companies must be in order to enable them to pay this 1\ per cent. I quite frankly believe that, by comparison, Shylock must be deemed to have been a kindly old gentleman.
The minister suggests that we cannot place these companies under the general definition of banks, but I suggest that is a point that is
Bank Act
arguable. In spite of that fact, we are asked to adopt the negative measure called deposit insurance under the name of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. I should like to know why legislation regarding this Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation is not before us at this time, because the rules and regulations of that deposit insurance corporation are part and parcel of the supervision to which the minister referred in his statement at the resolution stage.
Let me use the minister's words. He said that this whole situation must be subject to effective inspection and adequate regulation in order to safeguard depositors, primarily. Let me add these words, there must also be some safeguard for shareholders and creditors. What are those safeguards? Will the superintendent of banking under the federal government have authority to go into the operations and investment portfolios of these trust companies? What is to be the effective inspection? Does this so-called deposit insurance feature of the Bank Act merely involve the payment of a fee? If that is the case, it is meaningless and will only result in an additional cost to banks under federal charter, as well trust companies, which are already subject to federal inspection and safeguard.
So far as the general public is concerned, why should we ask the banks and trust companies incorporated under federal charter to announce that they have deposit insurance? The reaction of such announcement on the part of the average depositor will be negligible. The average depositor will ask: So what is new? Under any deposit insurance scheme it is the depositor who is the consumer, not the bank or the corporation or the trust company, and he is the one who will have to pay the fraction of 1 per cent, perhaps, for the insurance. A great number of Canadians are depositors in chartered banks and trust companies, and they will have to foot this bill because they are being asked to assume an additional cost, presumably to protect those individuals who are taking their money out of chartered banks and putting it in provincially incorporated trust companies.
Another feature of this insurance is that these trust companies must apply for an insurance certificate after obtaining the consent of the government of the province in which they are incorporated. This raises the speculation that a provincial government might decide that it is going to institute its own deposit insurance scheme. In that event trust companies may prefer to carry their

Bank Act
insurance with the federal deposit insurance scheme for the purposes of the liability, or as a selling point as far as the public is concerned. Surely this cannot add to the efficient function of deposit insurance if there is a provincial government veto.
Much can be said about the suggested interest formula.

There are many people who want to obtain money. There are provisions in this bill with regard to conventional mortgages on residential properties. There is a great shortage of money in this respect; there is tight money. Certainly the banks and related major trust companies may be able to alleviate this problem. But the point is that they must have the power; and until this bill is considered and implemented no action can be taken, either

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would reiterate what has been indicated by the Leader of the Opposition and my colleagues the hon. member for Perth, the hon. member for Northumberland and the hon. member for Kamloops, that this bill is just tinkering with the central theme of the Porter commission report. subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the
Official Opposition, I and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party have changed some of our views and have modified some of the views we expressed at the resolution stage. I have no apologies to offer for stating this position. I would, on the other hand, feel that I had a great many apologies to offer if, after almost three months of very intensive study and wide ranging discussions with economists, we had not found it necessary to perhaps modify at least the emphasis that we place on certain aspects of government policy.
Partly as a result of the debate we had on inflation and partly due to the current consumer price hearings, we have found ourselves driven to consider the Bank Act and its revision in a much wider context than that in which we had formerly considered it. The inadequacy of banking legislation alone as an efficient instrument of monetary policy has become more and more clear, and the need to link it with other government policies and activities has become clearer still.
It is true enough, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) says, that this bill must go before the committee, where it will be examined in detail and witnesses will be cross-examined, and it must then come back to the committee of the whole of this house for clause by clause discussion. There are, however, a number of definite principles involved in the bill which I think merit discussion, indeed require discussion, on second reading. I would say they were the following: the control of interest rates, the question of reserves, the matter of the control of "near banks", the question of deposit insurance, and the question of who is to operate the clearinghouse facilities in the financial system of the country. To these I would add something else which I think is very closely
October 5, 1966

related with banking policy on the part of the government, and that is what I would term their credit policies.
The more one studies the use of monetary policy, and in particular the use of interest rates, as a means of allocating resources in this country, the more he becomes convinced of its inadequacy, of its incapability to really make those sorts of allocations that most of us, I think, would wish to see. Of course, there is a very simple reason for this. There are many areas in our economy-and I have only to mention such things as housing, education, area development and those types of things-which are in the main largely unprofitable, or at least of very low and deferred profitability. As a consequence we feel that the Bank Act should be considered in the light of other government measures to be taken to offset the tendency of market forces to distort the allocation of resources, in contradiction of what would be desirable social objectives.
In dealing with the question of interest rates I think we must go far beyond the question of whether we are going to lift the 6 per cent ceiling, whether we are going to do it at once, in stages or by the particular formula that has been suggested by the minister. There are compelling arguments for the removal of the 6 per cent limit. There is no question about it, it has been a clumsy and unselective tool of control and one, moreover, that has been repeatedly evaded by the banks. To be fair to the banks, I think they have been driven to this evasion by recent developments in the financial community of Canada, the rise of the so-called "near banks." Nevertheless, it has meant in essence that the 6 per cent limit has been ineffective; that in essence, anyway, it has been incapable of doing the sort of job that requires to be done.
While, as I say, there are compelling reasons for its removal-and 1 have not found an economist who would dispute that statement-I have, on the other hand, found many economists who feel that in conjunction with the removal of the statutory limit the government should undertake a much wider responsibility in regard to interest rates than they have done hitherto. During the resolution stage I made somewhat the same suggestion, At that time I suggested there should be a regulatory body established to review interest rates, somewhat on the lines of other government regulatory bodies. But one result of the intensive discussions, thought and
Bank Act
study we have had for nearly three months was that we came to the conclusion that the regulatory body idea was too clumsy and too slow of operation, and that the Bank of Canada is the logical and obvious vehicle by which this government policy can be implemented.
You may ask: Just what would be the mechanism by which the Bank of Canada would exercise these new responsibilities? There are various ways in which it could be done. One might perhaps follow the example of the United States which has quite recently, within the last week or so, established controls at the other end of the interest ladder. They have established controls over the amount of interest that lending institutions might pay to attract depositors, with the idea-and I imagine it may very well be a successful idea-of thus limiting the amount they would be capable of charging for the loans they make to customers. However, I have no doubt whatever that there are a number of mechanisms that could be devised whereby the central bank could exercise the function of controlling interest rates throughout the economy.
We take this position because there seems no doubt whatever that if we are simply going to remove the interest rate from the banks we are inviting a sort of jungle warfare of interest rates to the great detriment of the Canadian economy. It seems to me to be far too simple a solution to a very complex and difficult situation, because there has grown up alongside the chartered banks a whole bevy of new banking institutions-I think that is the correct way in which to describe them-which are outside government regulations. The government take the position that to solve this problem, or at least to promote the idea of equity of treatment, it will remove the controls over the chartered banks so they will be, on that score at any rate, on an even footing with the "near banks". This to us seems to be a counsel of irresponsibility and that, rather than do that, the government should remove the present statutory lending limits and make the banks and all other lending institutions in the country subject to central bank control in respect of interest rates.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I want to come back again, Mr. Speaker, to the necessity of the government at the same time taking some other steps to control the marked distortion of credit which has been such a prominent feature in recent months of the Canadian economy. We had a witness

October 5, 1968
Bank Act
before the committee the other day who took the position that any rectification of wealth distribution or allocation of resources in this country should be effected, not by means of controlling selective controls, such as interest rates, but rather by more positive action on the part of the government, such as the use of agencies it now has. I suggest there should be perhaps one or more new agencies established for the funnelling of credit and funds into those areas which the government in its wisdom, and parliament in its wisdom, consider require special treatment. I have suggested some of them such as housing, education and area development.
I would add to that the possibility of establishing an agency to deal with some of the needs of provinces and municipalities, various local government bodies, in the provision of funds to them at interest rates that would be far below anything the market would provide, far below anything that would be reasonable for the Bank of Canada to establish as a general interest rate. These, I think, are equally important to the problem of controlling the interest rates of the chartered banks.
Now, with regard to the control of the "near banks", we feel it is essential that they should be brought under federal control. We feel that in conjunction with the federal control of interest rates, the minister's suggestion of deposit insurance is probably the best way of bringing them under federal control. I think we should not delude ourselves that because these institutions are not called banks, they are not actually banks. I take it that most people would agree that a suitable definition of a bank would be an institution which accepted deposits and which granted to its depositors chequing privileges.
In connection with this, I would suggest another means by which the "near banks" could be brought under federal control. I think the Porter commission recommended it in toto, but if not I would suggest that the operation of the clearinghouse should be removed from the control of the Bankers' Association and again placed in the hands of the central bank or an agency of the central bank. In that way, we can be sure that each financial institution which desires to offer chequing privileges, each financial institution that desires to receive the benefit of deposit insurance, will be obliged to submit itself to government inspection and to government regulation.
The hon. member for Edmonton West doubted the capacity of the inspector general

of banks to undertake the sort of inspection the minister has suggested. I, myself, cannot see any particular difficulty involved in this. I do not have the idea that the inspector general of banks goes around inspectnig every bank himself. He has a staff. I presume it is not beyond the capacity of Canada or this government to increase that staff to the necessary size for the sort of inspection of which the minister spoke.
I would go further on this question of insurance, and this has always been a favourite thought of mine with regard to our economy. If the government is going to establish a corporation that would provide insurance on deposits in lending institutions, then I see no reason why its powers should be necessarily severely and for all time limited to that field of insurance. Here, it seems to me perhaps the government might find itself making the first, timid step toward the development of a government insurance system in this country. This might very well solve some of the problems we face with regard to the allocation of resources in our economy.
Now, with regard to reserves, I imagine few people would quarrel with the statement that so far as the original purpose of establishing bank reserves is concerned, which was presumably to protect depositors, that role for reserves is pretty well gone. No one, I think, seriously imagines that a chartered bank in Canada is going to collapse. It is many years now since one did collapse. The reason, of course, that they are safe from collapse is that they automatically come to the rescue of each other when it is necessary to do so. This is quite right, and should be done.
There is a role, however, for reserves, and that is in regard to the regulation of the total money supply. It has not been used, within my knowledge, to any great extent within recent memory, but it is always a weapon in the hands of the central banks if other methods of controlling total money supply should fail or falter. We feel the Bank of Canada should have much wider powers with regard to the control of reserves than is suggested in the minister's bill. It should be entirely at the discretion of the central bank to decide what reserves should be at any one particular point. If it is going to be used as an instrument of monetary policy, and that really is its only function now to help control money supply, then the central bank needs to be able to act much more quickly than is envisaged in the minister's bill.
October 5, 1966

Bank Act
I would agree with the minister on one thing. If we are retaining the reserves, then there should be complete public disclosure of their volume and nature. No longer should we allow these things to be hidden behind some veil of secrecy, in the so-called public interest. The public has a right to know how much the banks are making and what it is costing the people of Canada to maintain their very efficient banking system. These things should not be left in the midst of speculation.
Now, I want to return, Mr. Speaker, to the suggestions I made in connection with the elimination of the 6 per cent interest rate. I make this quite clear to the house. While the members of the New Democratic Party feel that in all intelligence and logic the removal of the 6 per cent blanket interest ceiling on the chartered banks should be removed, and there is no rational economic argument for retaining it, nevertheless we are not prepared to support that removal unless the government is prepared to take these ancillary actions; unless it is prepared to enter much more widely and much more effectively into the whole region of interest control than it has done in the past, to take responsibility for levels of interest in this country; unless it is at the same time prepared to make these changes in the fiscal and taxation structure that will require a greatly increased incursion of government into the field of funnelling credit into those areas of the economy which are now starved by market conditions.
We feel that such agencies as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Industrial Development Bank, the Farm Credit Corporation, to name but a few of them, must be strengthened financially and their scope very greatly enlarged. We realize, of course, that to do this effectively the government must get into its hands sufficient funds in order to carry out such a program. This, in turn will require very careful scrutiny of our taxation structure, such as has been made by the Carter commission. We hope that commission's report will be available to us before too long. Unless the government is prepared to take these other steps for the control of interest rates, this party does not feel it can support the mere blanket removal of the ceiling of 6 per cent on bank loans.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I would hope that at some time or other before the conclusion of this debate, and prior to our voting on the matter, the minister might indicate whether the government
was prepared to undertake this control of interest rates throughout the economy. Otherwise, I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that we shall have to take steps to make perfectly clear our opposition to the mere removal of the 6 per cent rate, and then let the jungle warfare start. Because that, of course, is what is going to happen. No one can convince me, and I am sure nobody would be able to convince any of the economists to whom I have spoken, that the removal of the 6 per cent ceiling, without some compensating action on the part of the government, will have any effect whatever except that of letting loose a battle of interest rates that may well be disastrous for our economy.
I would hope that when the bill comes before the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs we might get an answer to many of the questions that I and others have raised; that we might have a rather clearer idea of just how the central bank intends to operate; that we might have witnesses from the chartered banks whom we can question on some of the aspects of their operations.
I have always felt, Mr. Speaker, that the revision of the Bank Act provides an opportunity once every ten years to give a quick educational seminar course to members of the House of Commons, which is much required. In fact, I think there might be some ground for suggesting that for this purpose we should have one every year. Anything that will expand our knowledge of this extremely complex and intricate subject is to be desired.

He was the major speaker on this bill when it was brought before the house for first reading.
I am sorry to say that the hon. member for Edmonton West is still on the old bandwagon. It has very faded colours now and has lost some of its tires, and in a few years time it will probably still be working with the same broken spokes. The reason we never arrive at any solutions to some of the problems facing us today is that we have never dared do anything new in this field. Progress has been made and the Canadian people have been developing the country, but in the financial

field this progress in science, and these developments have preserved their status quo. This, Mr. Speaker, can only be a handicap and prevent our economic advancement in the over-all picture.
I told the minister, Mr. Speaker, when I took part in the debate on inflation, and also when the bill came before the house for first reading, that I would take the opportunity to speak only briefly on second reading, but that in the committee stage I, and also some of my colleagues and other members, intended to discuss thoroughly each clause of the bill, and all the connotations. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the government airport concession operations regulations to provide, by virtue of its power to regulate the performance of any service for persons on the airport, that no licence be granted by Her Majesty in Right of Canada for the operation of insurance vending machines.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution, in short, calls on the Government of Canada to give consideration to amending the airport concession operations regulations to prohibit in air terminals, all of which are run by the Government of Canada through the Department of Transport, what we see in every air terminal, namely air flight insurance vending machines.
This resolution is introduced by myself on behalf of the air line pilots, engineers, cabin attendants, and stewardesses who must board their aircraft knowing that the danger of
October 5, 1966

take as much as 60 per cent. These rentals amounted in Canada to $158,000 in 1965. That does not even cover the cost of one crash investigation, according to the civil aviation director of the Department of Transport.
I am not against travel insurance itself. I have no objection to a man, anxious about travelling, obtaining travel insurance through his regular insurance agent. The agent either knows him or can have an investigation made concerning him.
The potential saboteur knows that if he buys a policy beyond his means, or if death occurs soon after he has taken one out, questions will be raised. It is true that other insurance policies allow a would-be murderer, or someone bent on self-destruction to fake a car accident or something similar; but only flight insurance is tailored to mass murder.
Airport trip insurance, because of its nature, offers temptation to unstable people. It has been described as an invitation to maniacs, because of the incentive it affords. There are several reasons for its inherent danger. It is easily accessible to anyone, regardless of his mental or emotional condition; its acquisition requires only a handful of loose change, making it an attractive gamble; it can be purchased on the spur of the moment; it can be purchased in virtual anonymity; it lacks the screening safeguards normally associated with the sale of other types of insurance.
The problems associated with the sale of insurance at airports do not arise with regard to other forms of travel insurance. A bomb placed aboard a train or ship is not likely to kill everyone on board, as a bomb which explodes in a plane is likely to do. The fact that policies are uncollectable if it is the purchaser who is responsible for death is not a deterrent. Anyone who plans to destroy a plane does so in the hope that his crime will go undetected, because of the very nature of air travel. That is, the murderer must rely on a complete destruction of the aircraft along with the death of everyone on board to prevent his crime being discovered.
A former United States federal aviatior. agency administrator has called flight insurance a "gyp". The odds against being killed in an air crash in Canada are 276,000 to one. Flight insurance pays off at 30,000 to one, or only a tenth of the true odds.
Accidental death and double indemnitj policies, which are more normal, pay off at about half the true odds. True they are more
October 5, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES
expensive-$35 a year for $30,000 coveragi
but they are payable for any accidental death, the chances of which are one in 1,755 per year, compared to one in 276,000 for a plane trip.
Economics professor Dr. Robert Easnir of Northwestern University claims that the purchaser of air accident insurance has tended on the average to pay four to five dollars in premiums for every one dollar paid out. Flight insurance therefore has a loss ratio, that is, a percentage of premiums paid out in benefits, amounting to only 25 per cent compared with the average in the industry of 70 per cent.
Of the 403 people killed in Canada in the last 20 years, only 40 held flight insurance. Twenty two people were needlessly killed in the Guay case alone. In other words, 22 died so that the estates of 40 others might be fattened by flight insurance.
It has been proven that air travel is the safest way to travel. The danger to passengers is greater on a train, in a bus or in the family car. But insurance is not sold at railway or bus terminals or at wayside gas stations. Why, then, should insurance be sold at airports? There is no reason for it. Flight insurance is unnecessary and merely pampers the fear some people have about flying.
The danger of flight insurance has been examined on many occasions. In 1962 a United States committee of aviation officials, air line representatives and insurance executives noted that in five accident cases which they studied the desire to profit from flight insurance was the predominant motive. Many of the air line staff associations have passed resolutions on the subject, including the International Federation of Air Line Pilots Association meeting in March, 1965 in the United States. Bills have been introduced in the United States Senate having the same purpose as the resolution which I have brought before the house this afternoon.
The whole subject is being studied by the Canadian Bar Association's air law sub-committee; it is being studied by the Canadian Coroners Association, which is equally concerned about the connection between trip insurance and sabotage. I suggest that the parliament of Canada should also be concerned. I hope this resolution will be passed today, so that there can be consideration in Canada of the vital safety issue involved in the machine vending of flight insurance.

speechtext:
My
main point in rising today is to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard on having brought this important matter to the attention of the house and therefore, we hope, to that of the country. I think his observations are most timely, and they may become even more timely as these tragic accidents continue to occur.
To me, the present "punch board" method of selling flight insurance at airports is something which calls for a hard second look. Apart altogether from the method of selling this insurance, I think we might well consider the type of insurance which is marketed. It is now possible for a person to purchase a large amount of insurance on the life of a person who is not even related to him. I think it would be a safety factor if there were a provison that persons outside the immediate family of the purchaser could not be insured.
I suggest, also, that instead of the fantastic sums of money for which purchasers can insure other people's lives, a reasonable amount should be made available to the survivors-the family-together with something by way of a monthly income to replace the lost breadwinner's earnings.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This whole subject is one of very real public interest, and rather than see the notice of motion talked out I shall conclude by urging hon. members to refer the matter to a committee, such as the committee on justice and legal affairs, where a study in depth can be made of it.

subtopic: SUGGESTION TO REFUSE LICENSING OF INSURANCE VENDING MACHINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover of this notice of motion for bringing to public attention a matter which certainly should be of concern to parliament, and which is of real concern to pilots and others who work on our air lines. Too often matters such as this are buried by being talked out, but I hope this will not meet that fate but will be referred to a committee where the subject can be fully explored.

Suggested Removal of Flight Insurance
As is often the case, this motion proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) in itself does not adequately cover the problem. The purpose of notices of motions is to bring matters to public attention and encourage discussion of them. That is what I hope this notice of motion will do.
Much of what the hon. member said applies to air trip insurance. Although I understand that there may be a certain extra attraction offered by slot machine insurance to a deranged mind, I believe consideration of the problem should include air trip insurance generally.
Although the hon. member referred to studies being conducted elsewhere, and to bills which have been introduced in the United States Congress, I believe remarkably little consideration has been given to the problem. The Canadian Bar Association discussed it at some length at its annual meeting in 1965, but reached no conclusions. I understand the consensus was that a full study should be made by the association's air law provincial subcommittees, but so far as I am aware no report has been produced leading to any specific recommendation from the association.
The bills which have been presented in the United States Congress seem to be pretty much in a deep freeze. I understand three identical bills have been introduced in the House of Representatives. I believe they would void all contracts of insurance covering loss of life or personal injury which purport to limit coverage to a specific trip. One bill would reduce the amount of flight insurance which passengers could purchase at airports, and limit the liability of insurance vendors to a maximum of $50,000 for the death of each passenger. However, none of these bills is likely to be discussed in detail in the near future. All have been referred to the house committee on commerce, but no hearings have been scheduled on any of them.
One reason may be that the federal aviation agency of the United States government conducted a detailed study of air line sabotage about a year ago, and reached the conclusion that air line saboteurs are beyond the reach of any reasonable approach and the removal of airport insurance vending machines would not achieve the purpose intended. It also concluded that the profit motive is universally recognized as one of the causative factors in sabotage, as it is in homicide generally. Air trip insurance has been a factor in some of
[Mr. Stanbury.l
the air line sabotage cases which have occurred in the United States.
Another conclusion was that normal insurance coverage should not be suspended during air line flights. This would be unreasonable because insurance is a definite benefit to survivors of air crash victims, whose interests would not be served by a flat exclusion rule.
A third conclusion was that air trip insurance should not be eliminated, nor should the sale of insurance at airports be limited. The agency noted that sabotage usually required prior planning, and the sale of insurance at airports would not be a major factor in such prior planning. It concluded that there was no evidence that past sabotage would not have occurred but for insurance, or that future sabotage would be eliminated or diminished by the abolition or curtailment of insurance. It reasoned that the insurance benefits outweighed the speculation that sabotage might be curtailed or lessened by restrictions on, or the abolition of, insurance.
It also decided that the amount of trip insurance available to each individual should not be limited, and that the ready availability of other types of insurance made the value of such limitation highly speculative.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the latest advice given to the United States government is that the suspension of air trip insurance is not to be recommended. However, I do not think we should rely on that. I believe the Canadian parliament should receive the advice of responsible authorities in this country, including the advice of the coroners, of the Canadian Bar Association, and of all groups who have indicated a concern with this matter. The most appropriate way of getting this advice would be through the standing committee on justice and legal affairs.
I hope the subject matter of this notice of motion will be referred to that committee. I also hope that committee will go into the matter thoroughly, dealing not only with the question of the sale of insurance through vending machines at airports, but with all air trip insurance and its effect on air line sabotage. I support the intent of the motion to stimulate the most far-reaching discussion and consideration of the problem and I hope it will receive that kind of study in committee.

subtopic: SUGGESTION TO REFUSE LICENSING OF INSURANCE VENDING MACHINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with other hon. members in congratulating the hon.
October 5, 1966

member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Bas-ford) on introducing this notice of motion. Like other hon. members I hope it sparks a certain amount of public discussion of a serious problem, but I for one remain to be convinced that it is as serious a problem as has been suggested by some speakers to day. I think it would be a great injustice to a great many people who travel by air if this type of insurance were removed from easy access.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Members of parliament, for example, do a great deal of travelling, particularly those on the west coast, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), no doubt is aware, and if we were not able to buy this type of insurance it would then be necessary for us to go to an agent to obtain it. The rates of these agents would be very high, simply because the insurance rates would be based upon the number of miles flown and on the number of trips we take in areas where the incidence of accident is high. I think it would be an imposition if this method of buying insurance were removed from the airports. By this method people who make occasional trips and who feel queasy, who are not familiar with flying, who are not convinced it is the best way, but find themselves in the position of having to fly, are in a position to protect their families in case of accident.
The accident rate for air lines is very low. I am told that flying is the safest way to travel. We are entering into a new era of subsonic and supersonic transportation. We hear that the jumbo jets will be with us in 1971, and we understand that supersonic jet travel will be available shortly thereafter. So, these new methods of flying, combined with the phenomenal increase in air line passenger and freight traffic create a certain difficulty with respect to our airports, overcrowding of the skys and overcrowding of terminal facilities. Even though the air lines so far have maintained an excellent record of safety, I think we also have to be aware that with the projected increases and the overcrowding that is taking place in the skies today, the incidence of legitimate accidents quite possibly will rise and that this ability to buy insurance over the counter at airports is convenient and is something the removal of which I think we should consider very carefully. Whether or not this opportunity for benefit should be removed because of fears, legitimate or otherwise, of the possibility of
8367
Suggested Removal of Flight Insurance someone killing his wife with a bomb in an airplane, I am not prepared to say at this time; I have not made up my mind.
But there are arguments on the other side. Certainly the danger of this sort of thing happening in the supersonic pressurized aircraft we have today is of a different order than when we were flying in the DC-4's and 6's which were not pressurized. A small bul-lethole in a pressurized cabin at 45,000 feet has a strong possibility of being fatal, but the same accident in the old aircraft was not quite as dangerous. The hon. member who introduced this gave us the example of the fellow who blew out the wall in the washroom. He stated that in a DC-8 or 9 there would have been a fatality; the whole plane would have cracked up simply because of the type of aircraft construction being used.
The other point to which I would offer a certain amount of objection is that of motive. I do not think all crimes are committed as a result of a greed for money. There are other motives. You may want to get rid of your wife or she may want to get rid of you, and this would be an opportunity. You might want to get rid of somebody else on the aircraft. Money is not the only motive. I think human nature is much more complex than is suggested by those who put forth the example of the economic man.
The second point is that in the description given by the hon. member these are the people who do these things. I think his argument fails when one recognizes the fact that their motive is not necessarily money. My feeling is that money is only incidental. Like most people who take a flight and feel queasy, who find the sky not as quiet as they would have like it, and who, before they step into the aircraft, invest a half a dollar in insurance, the person who plants a bomb in the aircraft also walks up and puts 50 cents in the machine. But I do not think that is the main motive.
As I said before, the air lines have a very good record of safety and efficiency. In the annual report of Air Canada for 1965 percentage statistics are given. I should like to read some of these into the record, because they indicate in one sector the improvement in service as well as the great number of passengers carried. In the last year, 1965, Air Canada carried 4,753,395 passengers on scheduled and charter services. This is an increase of 13 per cent in 1965 over 1964. As a matter of fact the actual increase in the
October 5, 1966
8368	COMMONS
Suggested Removal of Flight Insurance number of passengers carried exceeded Air Canada's expectations rather substantially. They were caught in many cases and are being caught today at peak periods, as I am sure hon. members who have tried to get out of Ottawa have found.
The Air Canada report goes on to suggest the situation was general throughout the industry and that all major air carriers faced this problem. Total seat miles for Air Canada were 5,458 million, an increase of 18 per cent, while revenue passenger miles flown exceeded 3,542 million, an increase of 21 per cent. The interesting statistic is that the passenger load rose from 63 per cent in 1964 to 65 per cent in 1965. Then, a few pages later appears a rather interesting statement:
The air line completed 98 per cent of Its scheduled mileage, maintaining its world-wide reputation for operating reliability. The credit is shared by the aircraft and the highly qualified employees who maintained, serviced and operated them.
1 gather that the 2 per cent difference between perfection and the actual showing was due to cancellations because of bad weather and not because of accidents or sabotage.
The argument in the motion as put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is that the type of person who indulges in this sabotage has a monetary motive. I think the reaction of the committees which have looked into this situation has been that money is not the prime motive and that the removal of these things would not provide a deterrent to potential saboteurs.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The second point, obviously, is that this is not the only source of insurance. It seems to me that if anybody is going to blow up an aircraft with dynamite or some other explosive, there is a good deal of planning which has to go into it; it is not something which is done on the spur of the moment. This requires a certain amount of initiative, planning and foresight, and perhaps a certain amount of nerve. We probably are not aware of the number of times that such an act of sabotage has been planned, and abandoned at the last moment because of a lack of courage.
By removing these machines from airports I do not think it will logically follow that such attempts will cease; but I feel that if we do that, other types of air transportation insurance should also be banned, whether the


aircraft is transporting passengers or goods. Such a step I believe would be unreasonable, because by banning the issuing of insurance for transportation you cannot prevent such acts from taking place.

subtopic: SUGGESTION TO REFUSE LICENSING OF INSURANCE VENDING MACHINES
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
