speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: SUGGESTION TO REFUSE LICENSING OF INSURANCE VENDING MACHINES
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman differentiate between airport counter flight insurance sales and insurance dispensed by machine? Does he not agree that there is a great difference? After all, what is really being expressed by this bill is a request that we consider the desirability of banning insurance vending machines for the reasons suggested.

subtopic: SUGGESTION TO REFUSE LICENSING OF INSURANCE VENDING MACHINES
speechtext:
I do not think there is an appreciable difference between going to a counter where there is a young lady, often very pretty, selling insurance, and buying insurance from a vending machine. I can obtain the same insurance from a girl at a counter as I can obtain from a machine. It is actually what is being sold and the circumstances of the sale to which I object. There is a warm, human and personal touch when one buys insurance at a counter as opposed to the impersonal efficiency of the machine. My point is that if you ban the sale of air transport insurance by a girl at a counter or by a machine at an airport, then you should go to the logical extreme of banning entirely this type of insurance in order that people will not resort to the type of sabotage under discussion.
It is my opinion that a great deal of planning and ingenuity must take place before anyone plans the destruction of an aircraft in order to obtain insurance, and that denying travellers the right to purchase insurance against accidents will not change the mind of an individual who intends to cause one.
I am in full agreement with the thought which has been expressed, that this subject should be referred to a committee of this house for deeper consideration and study. Most of the arguments that were presented in this regard were one-sidedly in favour of this suggestion, and I am trying to present the other side, so to speak.
It is my hope that it will be possible for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) or the
October 5, 1966
Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) to consider seriously the subject matter of this bill, particularly with regard to possible amendments, before it is sent to a committee, so that the subject can quite properly be investigated by the experts.
One of our problems in the House of Commons in discussing certain matters, keeping in mind our duties as members, is that we never have time to research these matters to the depth they deserve. A great many Canadians are travelling more and more by air, and for this reason this subject needs a great deal of investigation.
In recent days we observed the adoption by the United States authorities of greater safety features in automobiles. I believe this is long overdue, and that it will result in a substantial improvement in our automobiles in the next few years. The same situation in the matter of safety features does not exist in respect of the manufacture of aircraft. I cannot think of any aircraft accident in recent years due to a mechanical failure, and this is a very happy and satisfactory situation.
My belief is that a committee set up by the government or a government department should make an investigation into this whole matter relating to the growing risks of air travel. The proposed narrowing of air lanes from 120 miles to 90 miles recently received publicity. This has been referred to by experts, and particularly by pilots who fly these aircraft, as something that should be investigated. I am not sure that any government department is looking into this situation with any thoroughness. The supersonic age will be upon us in full force within the next six years and I am wondering whether or not a government department in Canada should look into this matter of urgency.
In conclusion I should like to make a plea to the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General, or the authority under whose jurisdiction this subject should fall, to give serious consideration to sending this whole matter to an appropriate committee in order that we can make a complete investigation.

I know an M.P. who quite recently went overseas. All he was required to do to purchase insurance on this basis was sign a form. I am sure the vendors of this type of insurance would consider a member of parliament to be a reasonably responsible person, although on occasion I have doubts about that. But surely there should be some kind of investigation, regardless of who is applying for insurance.
I congratulate the sponsor of this resolution for bringing its subject matter to the attention of the house, and I trust it will be considered by an appropriate committee. The result of such a study might be a recommendation to the house requiring the sale of this type of insurance to be made under circumstances which could prevent the occurrence of those things mentioned in the motion.

Mr. Speaker, this is another of those resolutions that could not possibly be adequately discussed, with all its ramifications, in the one hour allotted by the rules of the House of Commons. It is an extremely important resolution and should be given further study by members of the house.
As a traveller who has flown many, many, thousands of miles on our air lines since the end of the last war, I find myself deeply concerned about the problem of sabotage on aircraft. I have never, on entering an airplane, had any real concern about the ability

8370	COMMONS
Suggested Removal of Flight Insurance of the man in charge, the pilot, at the front end of the aircraft. As a matter of fact, I think it would be safe to say that I have flown many thousands of miles in the mountains of British Columbia when the pilot has found it safer, if you can conceive of this prospect, to stay down, even with a two-engined or four-engined plane in the mountain regions-that is to say, down in the river gorges-rather than up through a cloud bank and over the peaks of the mountains, because of the difficulty of returning to that height and the scheduled air route.
The pilot is the man in charge, and I have had no concern when this has happened because I have known that quite often he was a younger man than I and perhaps had more to live for than I had. But it now becomes a matter of great concern to the air line pilots themselves. When the Canadian Pacific Airlines plane went down in northern British Columbia-and I would say here, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian Pacific Airlines have an excellent record in flying the mountain regions and have not had any serious accident as a result of pilot error-investigations showed that there was some evidence of explosives having been placed on the plane. Immediately upon the report of that investigation the air line pilots issued a statement suggesting that there should be a law in Canada, and of course elsewhere, to provide that trip insurance should not be sold at airports. I do not recall that they singled out vending machines. I believe the concern of the air fine pilot is the fact that trip insurance is available; that is, that anyone may determine to purchase insurance that gives an extreme rate of return for a very small investment. This is their chief concern.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this resolution really does not go far enough. It may be regrettable that some of the pretty girls referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) would no longer be employed at our airports. But I am sure that with their ability and recognized good looks they would have no difficulty in obtaining employment with the car rental companies, and so on. We should have no real concern in this respect. The air line pilots are really concerned about this problem and I believe the public should become concerned about it. I think that people who are not adequately insured should not attempt to drive on the Queensway in Ottawa this afternoon between four o'clock and six o'clock. I
